extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of natural philosophy, history of science, and readers of Bacon's Novum Organum
extracted.subtask_description: Enumerating and analysing species of natural 'motions' (motus), their causes, interactions, and experimental tests; includes methodological guidance for investigating predominance and transmission of forces in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish biological vs chemical causes (fermentation/yeast)
rubrics_metrics.description: The generally received opinion ... is that [fermentation/yeast] is due to a chemical action set up by the life processes of minute organisms. The opposed view, attributing these changes entirely to chemical and physical forces, seems to have been set aside by recent experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify fermentation and related phenomena by investigating whether living organisms with self-multiplication are operative (biological cause) or whether purely chemical/physical forces suffice. Consult experimental literature (e.g., Pasteur) and use controlled experiments to discriminate causes. Example references given: Watts' Dictionary of Chemistry, article 'Fermentation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate spontaneous (biological) vs artificial (chemical) coagulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The coagulation of milk, when spontaneous, is also probably due to chemical action set up by minute living organisms. But, when produced by artificial means, as by an acid, the phenomenon is purely chemical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing coagulation, determine whether it occurs spontaneously (implying microorganism activity) or is induced by added reagents (purely chemical). Use this as a criterion to assign phenomena to biological or chemical classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify poisons into three causal types
rubrics_metrics.description: We must distinguish three cases. Some poisons, like vaccine virus, are due to the indefinite self-multiplication of low organisms within the body. Others, like arsenic, act purely chemically. Lastly, a third class, like chloroform or prussic acid, act ... physiologically, by destroying the dynamical activity of some tissue or organ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For toxicological classification, determine whether the agent's effect arises from biological multiplication, direct chemical action, or physiological disruption of tissues. This taxonomy guides investigation and treatment strategies; consult physiology (e.g., Carpenter) for mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test dependence on original impression to classify motus
rubrics_metrics.description: 'This 'motus' is distinguished from the two last by the continuance of the original impressions being necessary to the continuance of the effects. Thus light or sound ceases, when the source of the impression is withdrawn.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimentally remove or stop the source of a supposed 'motion' (e.g., light, sound, heat) and observe whether the effect persists. If the effect ceases immediately on removal, classify it as dependent on the original impression (motus impressionis); if it persists, classify differently (motus excitationis/assimilationis). Allow for propagation delay in light/sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish resonance (renewal) from continuous sound
rubrics_metrics.description: Illud autem manifestatur ex sedatio sive cohibitione corporis percussi. Si enim sistatur et detineatur campana fortiter et fiat immobilis, statim perit sonus; ... illa resonatio non est idem sonus numero, sed renovatur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To tell resonance from sustained sound, prevent the struck object's continued vibration (e.g., immobilize a bell or touch a string after strike). If sound ceases, the continued effect was resonance (renewal by object vibration), not a persisting original sound in the air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider configuration/situs (motus configurationis) in explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Motus Configuratiouis, aut Situs ... per quern corpora appetere videntur, non coitionem aut separationem aliquam, sed situm, et collocationem, et configuratiouem cum aliis. This 'motus' may be illustrated by the form of crystals, or the cellular structure of animals and plants, or the tendency of each particular species to assume a definite shape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing natural bodies and their tendencies, examine their spatial arrangement, shape, and internal configuration (cells, fibres, crystal forms). These configurational aspects can determine behaviour and must be investigated for proper understanding and manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match medium to the virtue for transmission (motus pertransitionis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aliud enim medium luci convenit, aliud sono, aliud calori et frigori, aliud virtutibus magneticis, necnon aliis nonnullis respective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a given medium is appropriate for the phenomenon under study (light, sound, heat, magnetism, electricity). Use experimental tests in vacuo or varying medium density to determine transmission properties (e.g., light/heat can transmit in vacuum; sound cannot; electrical discharge may require residual gas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify ruling parts and hierarchical dominance (motus regius/politicus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Motus Regius ... per quern partes in corpore aliquo praedominantes et imperantes reliquas partes fraenant, subigunt, ordinant, et cogunt eas adunari, separari, consistere, moveri, collocari, non ex desideriis suis, sed prout in ordine sit et conducat ad bene esse partis illius imperantis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In complex bodies (especially organisms), identify dominant parts (e.g., 'spirits' in animals, heart/brain) that regulate, restrain, or command other parts. Determine their degree of control and how their presence or removal alters whole-body behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gather 'instantiae luctae' to determine predominance of virtues/motions
rubrics_metrics.description: Etenim instantiae luctae (quae indicant praedominantiam virtutum, et secundum quas rationes et calculos praedominentur et succumbant) acri et sedula diligentia undique sunt conquirendae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect decisive instances of conflicts between forces/virtues (cases where one force prevails over another) and record conditions (quantities, speed, auxiliaries, impediments). Use these empirical 'instances of struggle' to infer which motions/virtues predominate under what ratios and to build predictive calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine modes and ratios of succumbing (how motions give way)
rubrics_metrics.description: Etiam modi et rationes ipsius succumbentiae motuum diligenter sunt introspiciendae. Nempe, an omnino cessent, vel potius usque nitantur, sed ligentur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When one motion yields to another, determine whether it is extinguished, merely restrained, or bound/enslaved. Investigate whether apparent quiescence is real cessation or latent/organized restraint (bound motion). This distinction affects understanding of equilibrium and recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse rotational motion by nine differentiations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipit autem motus iste rotationis differentias novem. Primam, centri sui, circa quod corpora movent: secundam, polorum suorum, supra quos movent: tertiam, circumferentiae sive ambitus sui, prout distant a centro: quartam, incitationis suae, prout celerius aut tardius rotant: quintam, consequentis motus sui, veluti ab oriente in occidentem, aut ab occidente in orientem: sextam, declinationis a circulo perfecto per spiras longius aut propius distantes a centro suo: septimam, ... octavam, distantiae propioris aut longioris spirarum suarum ad invicem: nonam ..., variationis ipsorum polorum ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying rotation, consider at least these nine aspects: the center of rotation, its poles, radius/circumference, angular speed, direction of revolution, deviations from a perfect circle (spirals), declination relative to poles, inter-spiral distances, and any polar variability. Use these dimensions to characterise and compare rotational phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quantitative comparisons of forces to predict dominance
rubrics_metrics.description: Exempli gratia: magnes ... detinet et suspendit ferrum, ad sexagecuplum pondus ipsius; ... Vectis tanti roboris sublevabit tantum pondus; ... Corium tensum ad tensuram talem non rumpitur; eo usque dominatur motus continuationis over motum tensurae; quod si ulterior fuerit tensura, rumpitur, et succumbit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predict which motion will prevail by quantitative comparison of weights, leverage, tensile strength, aperture size, and mixtures (e.g., explosive powders). Measure magnitudes (weights, tensions, sizes) and compare to known thresholds to determine whether one motion will dominate or succumb.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize apparent quiescence; assume latent microscopic motion
rubrics_metrics.description: In corporibus hie apud nos, nulla vera est quies, nee in integris nee in partibus; sed tantum secundum apparentiam. Quies autem ... latens processus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encountering macroscopic equilibrium, consider that it may be only apparent; investigate microscopic/particulate motion (latent processes) beneath the surface. This affects interpretation of stability, diffusion, and thermodynamic behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat speculative astronomical motions cautiously; defer to specialist observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sit Motus Decimus Octavus, Motus Trepidationis, cui (ut ab astronomis intelligitur) non multum fidei adhibemus ... The question of the existence or non-existence of trepidation could only be decided by a person conversant with the details of the received system of astronomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skepticism is advised for contested astronomical motions (e.g., trepidation). Decisions about such motions should rely on detailed astronomical observation and the expertise of astronomers rather than purely speculative natural-philosophical argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer plica materiae over a vacuum in explanations of density/spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: De illo nobis constat, rationem illam, propter quam introductum est Vacuum a Leucippo et Democrito ... falsam esse. Est enim plane plica materiae complicantis et replicantis se per spatia, inter certos fines, absque interpositione vacui.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When accounting for differences of density or apparent interstitial space in bodies, prefer the hypothesis that matter can fold/complicate itself ('plica materiae') rather than postulating true empty vacuum. Use experimental demonstrations (pneumatic properties) to evaluate such theoretical claims.
